results.title: GPU Prices 2026: H100 From $3.49/hr, RTX 5070 at +58%
results.author: Axis Intelligence Research
highlights:
> Prices verified on October 2, 2026. Every price on this page was read from the vendor’s live pricing page, public price API or retail listing on that date. AWS Capacity Block rates effective October 7, 2026 are taken from AWS’s own announcement on its pricing page.

Renting one NVIDIA H100 for an hour costs $3.49 on Runpod and $12.29 on Microsoft Azure — the same chip, listed on public pricing pages on October 2, 2026. Axis Intelligence Research’s GPU Hour Premium Ratio puts the hyperscaler list premium at 2.93x the neocloud median, and AWS is raising every GPU Capacity Block rate by roughly 15% on October 7.

## Quick Answer

How much does a GPU cost in October 2026? In the cloud, an NVIDIA H100 lists between $3.49 and $12.29 per GPU-hour on-demand; the neocloud median is $3.99. A B200 lists from $6.69 to $8.60. On the consumer side, the cheapest new RTX 5070 on Newegg was $869.99 against a $549 launch price — 58% above MSRP.

...

1. According to Axis Intelligence Research, hyperscalers list the NVIDIA H100 at 2.93 times the neocloud median price — $11.68 versus $3.99 per GPU-hour on-demand, as of October 2, 2026 (GPU Hour Premium Ratio, GHPR).
2. AWS raises EC2 Capacity Block GPU rates about 15% effective October 7, 2026, taking an H100 accelerator-hour from $5.191 to $5.970 and a B200 from $12.355 to $14.208, per AWS’s pricing page.
3. An 8-GPU H100 server rented on-demand for three years costs $2.58 million on Azure and $734,000 on Runpod, according to Axis Intelligence Research’s list-price TCO calculation.
4. The cheapest new GeForce RTX 5070 on Newegg cost $869.99 on October 2, 2026, 58% above the $549 price NVIDIA announced at CES in January 2025.
5. Azure’s spot price for an 8x H100 VM is 82% below its own on-demand rate — $18.17 versus $98.32 per hour in US East, per Microsoft’s Retail Prices API.

...

The H100 is the reference chip for AI compute pricing, and in October 2026 its price depends far more on who rents it to you than on the silicon.

### H100 on-demand price per GPU-hour by provider (October 2, 2026)

| Provider | Instance / SKU | Listed price | GPUs | Price per GPU-hour | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Runpod | H100 SXM Pod (Secure Cloud) | $3.49/hr | 1 | $3.49 | Runpod pricing |
| Lambda | NVIDIA H100 SXM instance | $3.99/GPU/hr | 1–8 | $3.99 | Lambda pricing |
| CoreWeave | NVIDIA HGX H100 (North America) | $49.24/hr | 8 | $6.16 | CoreWeave pricing |
| Google Cloud | a3-highgpu-8g, us-central1 | $88.49/hr | 8 | $11.06 | Google Cloud accelerator-optimized pricing |
| Microsoft Azure | ND96isr H100 v5, East US | $98.32/hr | 8 | $12.29 | Azure Retail Prices API |

Per-GPU-hour figures for 8-GPU instances are Axis Intelligence Research calculations: instance price ÷ 8. Google Cloud and Azure prices include the host vCPUs, memory and local SSD bundled into the VM; neocloud prices also bundle host resources, but in smaller amounts per GPU.

...

## Why Is AWS Raising GPU Prices in October 2026?

AWS publishes the reason in one line: Capacity Block reservation prices are dynamic and are updated periodically based on supply and demand. The October 7, 2026 update moves every GPU family up by the same proportion.

### AWS EC2 Capacity Block rate change, effective October 7, 2026

| Instance family | GPU | Rate before (per accelerator-hour) | Rate from Oct 7, 2026 | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | B300 | $14.040 | $16.146 | +15.0% |
| P6-B200 | B200 | $12.355 | $14.208 | +15.0% |
| P5en | H200 | $6.865 | $7.895 | +15.0% |
| P5e | H200 | $5.970 | $6.866 | +15.0% |
| P5 | H100 | $5.191 | $5.970 | +15.0% |
| P4de | A100 80GB | $2.214 | $2.546 | +15.0% |
| P4d | A100 40GB | $1.475 | $1.696 | +15.0% |

Source: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing, retrieved October 2, 2026. “Before” rates are the US East (N. Virginia) or US-region rates listed on the same page; percentage change is an Axis Intelligence Research calculation.

A uniform 15% move across seven GPU generations — including a 2020-era A100 40GB — tells you this is not a scarcity signal about one chip. Capacity Blocks are AWS’s mechanism for guaranteed short-term cluster access, and a flat repricing across the whole catalog reads as AWS re-pricing guaranteed availability itself. Buyers who only need interruptible capacity should read this as a reason to look at spot and neocloud rates, not as proof that GPUs in general got 15% more expensive.

## How Much Does a B200 or H200 Cost per Hour?

### Blackwell and H200 per-GPU-hour prices (October 2, 2026)

One detail that most rate cards hide: Lambda’s B200 is cheaper on-demand ($6.69) than in its own 1-Click Clusters ($8.87–$9.86). The cluster price buys guaranteed multi-node capacity with interconnect, not a per-GPU discount. Google Cloud does not list an on-demand price for its A4 (B200) VM at all; the cheapest public path is DWS Flex-start at $64.44 per 8-GPU hour.

results.title: Inside Google's TPU: How it works, and what it costs
results.author: Lorenzo Bradanini, Lorenzo Tettamanti
highlights:
- The compiler is on PyPI. Google’s TPU compiler ships inside libtpu, a 683 MB library, and compiles for TPUs that aren’t attached. We used it on a CPU-only container for v4, v5e, v5p, Trillium (v6e) and Ironwood (TPU7x).
- The critical batch. Trillium’s is 560, the highest of any shipping accelerator we have measured. Ironwood’s is 313 on Google’s datasheet and 270 by the compiler’s own constants, in the range of NVIDIA’s H100 (295) and B200 (281).
- The accumulator. In the final instruction stream for the same 1024³ bf16 matmul, Ironwood pops 1,024 results out of its matrix units and Trillium 4,096. Ironwood does no vector adds where Trillium does 3,072, and issues 80% fewer spill loads. Ironwood’s matrix instructions address a result buffer, `mrb[0]` to `mrb[255]`; Trillium’s results come out of an unaddressed queue.
- Precision. By the compiler’s cycle estimates, Ironwood runs an FP8 matmul in 0.48 times the cycles of bf16 and an int8 matmul in 1.13 times. On v5e, v5p and Trillium, int8 takes 0.47 to 0.62 times and FP8 e4m3 gains little. No chip the public compiler knows runs FP4 faster than its eight-bit path.
- Batch one. On v4 through Trillium, the compiler rewrites a batch-1 matmul into a vector multiply and reduction that its own cycle model prices at 2.75 to 3.50 times the matrix-unit version. One option turns the rewrite off. Ironwood doesn’t apply it.
- SparseCores. On Ironwood, every collective we compiled across four or more chips ran on the SparseCores, including the ragged all-to-all that MoE dispatch uses. The one exception was the dense all-to-all. No other generation offloaded anything. TPU 8i replaces those SparseCores with an engine built only for collectives.
- Storage. Arrays live in 4 KiB tiles, 128 elements wide. A single row of FP4 stores eight times its logical size. A KV cache with 64-wide heads costs twice its size in the row-major layout an attention kernel wants, and exactly its size in the layout the compiler picks when nobody asks.
- Prices. On Google Cloud’s on-demand rate card, the six accelerators we priced cost $1.40 to $1.65 per TB/s of HBM bandwidth per hour, TPU or GPU. Commitments follow a fixed formula: 70% of on-demand for one year, 45% for three. The estimated anchor rate for Anthropic is 13%.
- Money. Broadcom expects Anthropic to go from 1 GW of Ironwood in 2026 to 5 GW of TPU 8i in 2027 and 10 GW in 2028, and guides its AI revenue from $58 billion this fiscal year to $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Alphabet books multi-gigawatt TPU system sales in a $514 billion Cloud backlog and is raising up to $70 billion of equity for its build-out.

...

As of September, Google’s pricing page lists Ironwood at $12.00 per chip-hour on demand in Iowa, $8.40 on a one-year commitment and $5.40 on three years. 

Trillium lists at $2.70 on demand and $1.22 on three years, v5p at $4.20 and $1.89, v5e at $1.20 and $0.54. SemiAnalysis estimates that Anthropic pays about $1.60 per Ironwood chip-hour on Google Cloud. For GPUs on the same cloud, a September snapshot of public prices put an H100 at $5.38 and a B200 at $11.28 per GPU-hour on demand. 

The transacted neocloud market, as measured by Ornn’s index on 28 September, was $2.56 for an H100 and $8.11 for a B200.

Every hourly rate hides two prices. One is what you pay per unit of HBM bandwidth, which is what a decode step below the critical batch consumes. The other is what you pay per unit of compute, which is what you consume above it.

results.title: H100 rental price — what clouds charge per GPU-hour
results.author: Daniel Okafor
highlights:
AI chip explainers October 4, 2026 Updated October 19, 2026

# H100 rental price: what clouds charge per GPU-hour

The H100 rental price on the providers' own pricing pages runs from $1.78 to $11.06 per GPU-hour.

By Daniel Okafor 7 min read

The H100 rental price depends on the provider and on how you rent. On the providers’ own pricing pages, one Nvidia H100 ranged from $1.78 per GPU-hour, the lowest live ask on the Lium marketplace on October 19, 2026, to $11.06 on demand on Google Cloud, checked October 2. Among the clouds, CoreWeave spot was about $2.46, and Lambda and Nebius listed on-demand H100s at $3.99 and $4.50. These prices change often; the full, regularly re-checked list is on our cloud GPU price tracker.

...

Clouds publish H100 prices in two ways. Some list a price for a single GPU: Lambda shows its H100 SXM at $3.99 “/GPU/HR”, and Nebius lists the HGX H100 per GPU-hour. Others sell whole machines, usually eight H100s with CPUs, memory and local storage, and quote the machine’s hourly price. AWS, Google Cloud and CoreWeave do this. To compare the two, divide the instance price by the number of GPUs in it. CoreWeave’s 8-GPU HGX H100 instance lists at $49.24 an hour in North America, which works out to $6.155 per GPU-hour.

The division hides what else is in the box, and that differs by provider:

- Google Cloud’s a3-highgpu-8g (8 H100s) comes with 208 vCPUs, 1,871 GB of memory and 6,000 GiB of Local SSD, all included in its hourly price.
- CoreWeave’s HGX H100 instance includes 128 vCPUs, 2,048 GB of system RAM and 61.44 TB of local storage.
- Lambda lists its on-demand H100 SXM configuration with 208 vCPUs, 1,800 GiB of RAM and 22 TiB of SSD.

...

When you compare offers, compare the whole configuration, not the GPU line alone.

...

On-demand is pay-as-you-go: you start and stop instances and pay by the hour at the list price. All of the per-GPU figures from Lambda, Nebius and Google Cloud in the table below are on-demand.

Spot is spare capacity sold at a discount, which the provider can take back when it needs it.

...

Reserved and committed capacity trades flexibility for a lower or guaranteed rate. CoreWeave says committed usage brings “up to 60% discounts” on its on-demand prices. Google Cloud offers committed use discounts on its A3 machines; it says these machine types are not eligible for sustained use discounts or flexible committed use discounts.

...

## H100 prices on the providers’ pages

All figures below were read on each provider’s own pricing page on October 2, 2026, except the Lium row, which was read on October 19, 2026. Lium is a marketplace where the hosts set their own prices, so its figure is the lowest live ask at the time of reading and changes as machines are added and removed. Per-GPU-hour values for instance prices are the instance price divided by eight.

| Provider | Offer | Billing | Listed price | Per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lium | H100 80GB HBM3 (SXM), marketplace, lowest live ask | On-demand, billed per second | from $1.78 per GPU-hour (checked October 19, 2026) | $1.78 |
| CoreWeave | HGX H100, 8 GPUs, North America | Spot | $19.71 per instance-hour | $2.46 |
| Lambda | H100 SXM 80 GB | On-demand | $3.99 per GPU-hour | $3.99 |
| Nebius | HGX H100 | On-demand | $4.50 per GPU-hour (effective October 1, 2026) | $4.50 |
| AWS | p5.48xlarge Capacity Block, US East (N. Virginia) | Reserved, paid up front | $41.528 per instance-hour | $5.191 |
| CoreWeave | HGX H100, 8 GPUs, North America | On-demand | $49.24 per instance-hour | $6.155 |
| Google Cloud | a3-highgpu-8g, Iowa (us-central1) | On-demand | $88.49 per instance-hour | $11.06 |

Prices move in both directions and sometimes within days. Nebius’s table shows the HGX H100 at $3.85 per GPU-hour in its previous on-demand column and $4.50 in the column effective October 1, 2026. AWS’s P5 Capacity Block rate changes on October 7. Treat the table as a dated snapshot and check the cloud GPU price tracker for the current figures, which also cover Azure, RunPod, DigitalOcean, Crusoe, Hyperstack and other providers.

## What the hourly price leaves out

A GPU-hour price is rarely the whole bill.

- Tax. Lambda states its prices are “plus applicable sales tax/VAT/GST.” Most list prices are quoted before tax.
- Data transfer. CoreWeave says it charges “no ingress, egress, or transfer fees,” and Lambda advertises no egress fees. On clouds that do charge for data transfer, the charge is billed separately from the GPU-hour.
- Storage. Local SSD is part of several of the instance prices above, but persistent or network storage for datasets and checkpoints is priced separately.
- Operating system and software. AWS bills the Capacity Block operating system fee separately from the reservation fee, and lists different OS fees for Linux, RHEL, SLES and Ubuntu Pro.
- Region. Hyperscaler prices are per region. The AWS and Google Cloud figures above are for US East (N. Virginia) and Iowa respectively; other regions list different rates.

...

On the providers’ own pricing pages, from $1.78 per GPU-hour (the lowest live ask on the Lium marketplace, checked October 19, 2026) to $11.06 per GPU-hour (Google Cloud on demand, checked October 2, 2026). Among the clouds checked October 2, CoreWeave spot was about $2.46, and Lambda listed $3.99 and Nebius $4.50 per GPU-hour on demand. A marketplace ask changes as machines are added and removed.

results.title: Nebius did exactly what it said it would. Last week's Pulse flagged the on-demand increases Nebius had posted for October 1. Our October 4 catalog capture yesterday shows them in place, in … | Bobby Clay
results.author: Bobby Clay
highlights:
# Nebius did exactly what it said it would. Last week's Pulse flagged the on-demand increases Nebius had posted for October 1. Our October 4 catalog capture yesterday shows them in place, in … | Bobby Clay · LinkedIn · 2026-10-05T00:00:00+00:00

**Bobby Clay**.

---

Nebius did exactly what it said it would. Last week's Pulse flagged the on-demand increases Nebius had posted for October 1. Our October 4 catalog capture yesterday shows them in place, in dollars per GPU-hour:

H100: $3.85 to $4.50
H200: $4.50 to $5.40
B200: $7.15 to $8.50
B300: $7.85 to $9.50

That changed the lowest observed H100 list price across the nine providers we track. On September 27 it was Nebius at $3.85 per GPU-hour. On October 4 it was Crusoe at $3.90.
Everything else held. Of 14,001 GPU price listings in the October 4 catalog, 13,996 matched a September 27 listing, and the 20 Nebius listings were the only verified changes above 1%.

The transaction side moved on its own path. OCPI for H200 went from $4.84 on September 28 to $5.57 on October 4. Over the same stretch, the lowest H200 list price we track held at $4.29 (Crusoe). List prices and transaction prices measure different things, and this week the gap between them widened. If you buy on-demand capacity from a Neocloud, posted price notices are worth tracking. This one landed on schedule, to the cent.

The full issue, with every provider's lowest observed price and the method notes, is here:
https://lnkd.in/efqfwQWm

These are public catalog list prices, not live quotes, and a listing does not establish capacity or orderability.

results.title: Nebius and CoreWeave Lift Nvidia GPU Prices by Up to 21% - Daily Market Chronicle
highlights:
Nvidia rental prices are rising even for last-generation H100s. Nebius has posted an October 1, 2026 on-demand card that lifts selected Nvidia GPU-hour rates by 16.9% to 21.0%. CoreWeave said on September 17 that it is still signing compute at higher prices, including short contracts at about $40 million per megawatt of annualized revenue. A landlord can charge more for a chip it does not make only while that chip stays scarce. That is the signal behind Nvidia, and it is the opposite of a capacity glut.

Nebius’s price page, checked on October 2, still prints two columns. On-demand H100 is $3.85 per GPU-hour. The column marked effective October 1 is $4.50. The same split runs through the H200, the B200, and the B300. Reuters reported on September 17 that this was the second pay-as-you-go increase in about three months, with selected Nvidia GPU rates up 17% to 21%. The card on nebius.com/prices matches that range. It does not show every customer already paying the new rate.

## The card Nebius posted

Four Nvidia rows have a public before and after. GB200 NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 racks are still “contact us” in both columns. RTX PRO 6000 stays at $1.80. L40S “from” rates do not move. The hike lands on the accelerators customers are queued for.

| Nvidia GPU | Prior on-demand column | Announced October 1 card | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HGX H100 | $3.85 | $4.50 | +$0.65, or 16.9% |
| HGX H200 | $4.50 | $5.40 | +$0.90, or 20.0% |
| HGX B200 | $7.15 | $8.50 | +$1.35, or 18.9% |
| HGX B300 | $7.85 | $9.50 | +$1.65, or 21.0% |

Reuters’ “17% to 21%” is this range, with 16.9% rounded up. “Up to 21%” is the B300. The smaller H100 move is the one that changes the reading. Hopper is not the generation Nvidia is leading with. A prior-generation accelerator getting more expensive to rent is not what surplus hardware looks like.

...

Announced Nebius on-demand rates for October 1, 2026, set against the prior on-demand column still printed on the same page. These are posted card rates, not a receipt. The live page and a third-party tracker still disagree, so this chart does not show what every customer is paying. Source: nebius.com/prices, checked October 2, 2026.

...

## The announced column is not yet the only column

October 2 is after the effective date, and the page still shows both numbers. The left-hand label is still “On-demand, GPU-hour.” The right-hand label is “GPU-hour (Effective October 1, 2026).” A customer cannot tell, from the page alone, which figure the console will bill.

GPU Finder’s Nebius page, with availability checked at 06:23 UTC on October 2, still listed one-GPU on-demand rates of $3.85 for the H100, $7.15 for the B200, and $7.85 for the B300. Those are the old column. The same check already showed the H200 at $5.40, the new column, with a spot print of $2.45 beside it. The H100 spot print on that row was $2.15. The tracker has not frozen. It has moved one of the four headline GPUs and left the other three on the pre-October number. Treating the whole book as repriced at midnight on October 1 would be tidier, and it would be wrong.

Commitment discounts can run up to 35% below on-demand for large clusters reserved for multiple months. Full discount on the new H100 card is $2.93 an hour, under the old $3.85 list. On the new B300 card it is $6.18, under $7.85. “Up to” is not “everyone gets.” The headline increase is the unreserved rate.

Spot is a third price. Preemptible rates can change every 15 minutes, and the ceiling sits one cent under on-demand, but the printed floor is $0.79 on H100 and H200 and $0.99 on B200 and B300. An interruptible job is not paying $4.50. The October card is about firm capacity. Most revenue is priced as annual contract value per megawatt, not off this page.

...

Effective October 7, AWS says capacity-block rates per accelerator across available regions will be $5.970 on P5, $6.866 on P5e, $7.895 on P5en, $14.208 on P6-B200, and $16.146 on P6-B300, higher in GovCloud. On the US East H100 line, $5.191 to $5.970 is 15.0% on that reservation rate only. The same notice leaves on-demand and Savings Plan prices unchanged.

...

Did Nebius raise every GPU? No. H100, H200, B200, and B300 have higher October 1 figures. RTX PRO 6000 and the L40S “from” rates do not. GB200 and GB300 racks have no public hour.

Is $4.50 what an H100 customer pays? Not necessarily. The on-demand column still says $3.85, and GPU Finder still showed that H100 rate, plus B200 at $7.15 and B300 at $7.85, on the morning of October 2 UTC. It showed the H200 already at $5.40. Discounts of up to 35%, and dynamic spot, sit below either column.
